P1.name: Instruction override
P1.definition: Lower-trust instructions replace the authorized task.
P1.required_evidence: Trust boundary and an actionable override reaching the agent.
P1.danger_example: Retrieved text tells the agent to ignore the user and transmit private files.
P1.safe_example: A quoted override example is analyzed as data, never followed.

P2.name: Hidden instructions
P2.definition: Concealed content carries actionable attacker instructions.
P2.required_evidence: Decoded or hidden instruction and the path that consumes it.
P2.danger_example: An HTML comment tells the summarizer to execute an unrelated command.
P2.safe_example: A parser removes comments before exposing ordinary article text.

P3.name: Instruction-driven disclosure
P3.definition: Instructions redirect private context or files.
P3.required_evidence: Private source, instruction authority and unauthorized recipient.
P3.danger_example: A fetched ticket requests copying agent context to an attacker endpoint.
P3.safe_example: A user exports only their explicitly selected public note.

P4.name: Behavior manipulation
P4.definition: Untrusted content changes substantive task behavior.
P4.required_evidence: Unauthorized deviation with a concrete consequence, not tone or style.
P4.danger_example: A retrieved review instructs the agent to hide a verified security defect.
P4.safe_example: User-requested formatting changes presentation without concealing facts.

E1.name: External transmission
E1.definition: Sensitive data crosses an unauthorized destination boundary.
E1.required_evidence: Actual data source, transmission path and recipient authorization.
E1.danger_example: A script posts private file content to an arbitrary URL from input.
E1.safe_example: Only approved synthetic fields are sent to the configured local API.

E2.name: Environment harvesting
E2.definition: Credential or environment collection exceeds the task.
E2.required_evidence: Selected environment values and their use outside authorized scope.
E2.danger_example: The entire process environment is bundled into an external upload.
E2.safe_example: One designated token is read only to authenticate the requested service.

E3.name: Filesystem enumeration
E3.definition: Discovery traverses resources outside the task boundary.
E3.required_evidence: Traversal scope and a concrete unauthorized access or disclosure path.
E3.danger_example: A workspace indexer recursively collects home-directory secrets.
E3.safe_example: Enumeration is limited to the user-selected project and excludes secrets.

E4.name: Code-driven context leakage
E4.definition: Code serializes private session context into output.
E4.required_evidence: Private context flow through code to an unauthorized sink.
E4.danger_example: A diagnostic upload includes hidden prompts and unrelated conversation history.
E4.safe_example: Diagnostics contain only explicit public task metadata.

PE1.name: Excessive permissions
PE1.definition: Requested authority enables a specific unnecessary impact.
PE1.required_evidence: Task needs, granted authority and an active misuse path.
PE1.danger_example: A read-only helper grants an untrusted plugin write access to every repository.
PE1.safe_example: Read-only scope is restricted to the repository being inspected.

PE2.name: Privilege escalation
PE2.definition: Untrusted input reaches elevated execution beyond approval.
PE2.required_evidence: Privilege transition, attacker influence and boundary crossing.
PE2.danger_example: A root command accepts a user-controlled script path without validation.
PE2.safe_example: An authorized admin task runs a fixed command on disposable test data.

PE3.name: Credential access and persistence
PE3.definition: Secrets are exposed, misused or embedded insecurely.
PE3.required_evidence: A real secret or designated canary, its access path and unauthorized exposure.
PE3.danger_example: A usable hardcoded token is distributed in a public Skill or logged verbatim.
PE3.safe_example: Documentation uses an unmistakable placeholder; credentials stay scoped and unlogged.

SC1.name: Unpinned dependencies
SC1.definition: Mutable dependency resolution creates an actionable substitution path.
SC1.required_evidence: Install source, attacker influence and which acquired code executes.
SC1.danger_example: A privileged helper installs a mutable package from an attacker-controlled index.
SC1.safe_example: A vetted dependency is locked with a verified artifact digest.

SC2.name: Fetched script execution
SC2.definition: Downloaded code executes without an effective trust check.
SC2.required_evidence: Download source, verification and actual execution path; include reverse shells.
SC2.danger_example: An input URL is fetched and piped to a shell with access to private data.
SC2.safe_example: A fixed signed artifact is verified before controlled installation.

SC3.name: Obfuscated code
SC3.definition: Encoding conceals an actionable harmful operation.
SC3.required_evidence: Decoded behavior and reachable execution, not encoding alone.
SC3.danger_example: An encoded command is decoded and evaluated to launch a reverse shell.
SC3.safe_example: Base64 image data is decoded as bytes and never executed.

SC4.name: Namespace mismatch
SC4.definition: Identity confusion resolves a dependency to an unintended publisher.
SC4.required_evidence: Requested identity, resolver behavior and actual mismatched source.
SC4.danger_example: An internal package name resolves against an untrusted public fallback.
SC4.safe_example: The scoped package resolves only against its authenticated private registry.

SC5.name: Unverifiable install source
SC5.definition: An installation source lacks a usable trust basis.
SC5.required_evidence: Concrete provenance gap and its effect on executed dependencies.
SC5.danger_example: An installer follows an anonymous mutable redirect and executes the result.
SC5.safe_example: An internal artifact has a verifiable organizational signature.

R1.name: Untrusted input handling
R1.definition: Untrusted data reaches command, path, query or code sinks.
R1.required_evidence: Input source, sink and missing or bypassed validation.
R1.danger_example: A filename from JSON is concatenated into a shell command; traversal is also accepted.
R1.safe_example: Resolved paths remain under the allowed root and commands use validated argument lists.

R2.name: Dependency failure handling
R2.definition: A failed dependency makes a security-sensitive path fail open.
R2.required_evidence: Dependency error, fallback branch and concrete resulting unsafe operation.
R2.danger_example: A failed authorization API call defaults to permitting the requested deletion.
R2.safe_example: Authorization errors stop mutation and report failure.

R3.name: Resource exhaustion
R3.definition: Attacker-controlled work can exhaust a relevant bounded resource.
R3.required_evidence: Controllable size/count/depth and missing effective limits on an active path.
R3.danger_example: An archive is recursively expanded without limits into the shared task filesystem.
R3.safe_example: Expansion enforces size, count, depth and execution limits.

R4.name: Environment path injection
R4.required_evidence: Who controls the variable and which executable or resource it selects.
R4.danger_example: A privileged helper executes a binary from an attacker-writable PATH prefix.
R4.safe_example: The helper uses a fixed trusted executable and validates output destinations.

R5.name: Serialization integrity
R5.definition: Encoding ambiguity changes security-relevant data semantics.
R5.required_evidence: Producer/consumer mismatch and downstream authorization or execution effect.
R5.danger_example: Duplicate JSON keys make validation inspect one path and deletion consume another.
R5.safe_example: One strict parser rejects duplicate keys and the validated object is reused.

NR1.name: Network reconnaissance
NR1.definition: Discovery probes networks outside the authorized target scope.
NR1.required_evidence: Actual probe destinations, authorized scope and Skill attribution.
NR1.danger_example: A health-check Skill scans unrelated private subnets using user-controlled ranges.
NR1.safe_example: The user-authorized check contacts only its selected disposable service.
